newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee nations warn on supply as prices soar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee nations warn on supply as prices soar.

text.p: A bull market is raging in world coffee.

New York coffee futures on Wednesday extended the longest sustained rally in two decades. They were at the highest since frost last hit Brazil, back in 1994, even though this year's season for frost scares has yet to begin.
Supply is tight. America's stocks of arabica coffee beans are at 20-year lows. And speculators are on a buying spree.
Wednesday also saw London prices for the less-prized robusta coffees stand at new one-year highs. And retail values threaten to edge up again at the supermarket check-out.
"There is no more coffee in the producer countries," Guy-Alain Gauze, Commodity Minister of Ivory Coast, told Reuters in a Singapore interview.
"We are really facing problems with production".
Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation says it is finding it hard to meet export commitments.
"There's very little coffee in Colombia. The federation is having enormous difficulties meeting its commitments," its head, Jorge Cardenas, said on Tuesday.
Colombia is the number two coffee seller after Brazil.

Prices on New York futures for the arabica type of beans, mainly supplied from the Americas, have doubled this year. The July contract rose on Wednesday to the highest since mid-1994 at $2.48 cents per pound.
London brokerage GNI says speculative funds have "really got hold" of coffee futures now and that, with stocks low, talk of cold weather in Brazil will prey on traders' minds.
"A frost this year would cause chaos in world coffee markets," GNI said. "The market will therefore be incredibly sensitive to any frost threat over the next 15 weeks."
The 1994 frosts cut Brazil's 1995/96 crop by some 50 percent and sent futures to near 10-year highs. Since then, coffee has ridden a rollercoaster.
In the London market, for instance, trading the robusta beans that are widely used in instant blends, the 1994 frost and then drought in Brazil quadrupled prices to $4,140 per tonne.
But by early this year they had declined steadily to as low as $1,203. Then, as supply concerns reignited, the current new rally gathered momentum to take them back up.
Wednesday saw London hit $1,885.
Robustas, from Asia and Africa, have lagged New York arabicas in this year's rally, because they are in better supply.
But depleted roaster stocks have given producers everywhere the whip hand, says Celsius Lodder, executive director of the International Coffee Organization.
"The farmers will dictate the pace of everything." he said.
Western firms that have already had to lift retail prices include Folgers in the United States and Douwe Egberts, owned by U.S. giant Sara Lee Corp, in Europe.
Procter & Gamble Co's Folgers has raised the price $0.80 to $3.06 since March for a 13-ounce can.

According to the New York Times, the customer is now feeling the pinch. It quoted Allon Azulai, owner of Ozzie's Coffee with shops in Brooklyn, as saying he has raised the price of a cup of coffee by a dime.
"When I first opened, I was paying less than $4 for a pound of really good coffee," Azulai said, referring to wholesale costs. "Now it's up to $6 a pound"
A week ago, Douwe, leading roaster in the Netherlands, raised the Dutch price of a standard 250-gramme pack of coffee by 20 cents, its third rise this year.

It said in Amsterdam on Wednesday it could not rule out a further rise soon. "We are not translating these higher world prices into an increase in shop prices at the moment but we will do if it impacts on our costs," said spokesman Joost den Haan.
